q: What is an export?
r: A good or service sold to a buyer in another country
Exports bring money into the home economy.
w: A good or service bought from another country
A tax on goods crossing the border
A limit on goods allowed in

q: What is an import?
r: A good or service bought from a seller in another country
Imports bring foreign goods into the home market.
w: A good sold to a foreign buyer

q: What is a tariff?
r: A tax placed on imported goods
It raises the price of foreign products.
w: A limit on the number of goods imported
A ban on trade with a country

q: What is a quota?
r: A limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported
It restricts supply from abroad.

q: What is an embargo?
r: A government ban on trade with a particular country
It is often used for political reasons.
w: A limit on imports of one product

q: What is a subsidy?
r: Government financial support to a business or industry
It can make domestic goods cheaper.

q: What is the main purpose of a tariff?
r: To protect domestic industries and raise government revenue
It makes imports more expensive.
w: To lower the price of imports

q: What is a trade deficit?
r: When a country imports more than it exports
Imports exceed exports in value.
w: When a country exports more than it imports
When a country stops all trade
When a government spends more than it collects

q: What is a trade surplus?
r: When a country exports more than it imports
Exports exceed imports in value.
w: When a country has extra tax revenue
When a store has extra inventory

q: What is the balance of trade?
r: The difference between the value of a country's exports and imports
It can be a surplus or a deficit.
w: The total of all money in a country
That is not the balance of trade.
That is not the balance of trade.
That is not the balance of trade.

q: What is free trade?
r: Trade between countries with few or no tariffs or quotas
It encourages specialization.
w: Trade where all goods are given away
Free trade is not free goods.
It is not limited to one partner.

q: What is protectionism?
r: Policies that shield domestic industries from foreign competition
Tariffs and quotas are examples.
w: Policies that remove all barriers to trade
Policies that ban all domestic production

q: What does NAFTA's successor, the USMCA, cover?
r: Trade among the United States, Mexico and Canada
It updated the earlier trade agreement.
w: Trade among the United States, Japan and Korea
Trade within the European Union only
It does not involve the EU.

q: What is the World Trade Organization (WTO)?
r: An international body that sets and enforces trade rules among nations
It helps settle trade disputes.
w: A bank that lends to countries
A treaty that sets currency values

q: What does the International Monetary Fund (IMF) mainly do?
r: Promotes global monetary cooperation and supports countries facing financial crises
It lends to member countries.
w: Sets tariffs on imports for every country

q: What is the European Union (EU)?
r: A political and economic union of European countries with a single market
Many members share the euro.

q: What is a customs duty?
r: A tax collected on goods crossing a border
It is paid to the customs authority.
w: A fee for a store's license
It is not a license fee.

q: What is a letter of credit?
r: A bank's guarantee that a seller will be paid if conditions are met
It reduces risk in international sales.
w: A letter asking a customer to pay more
It is a guarantee, not a demand.
It is not a tax form.

q: What is a bill of lading?
r: A document issued by a carrier that acts as a receipt and contract for shipped goods
It lists the goods and destination.
w: It is not a tariff bill.
It is not a loan document.
It is not a tax return.

q: What are Incoterms?
r: Standard trade terms that define buyer and seller responsibilities in shipping
Examples include FOB and CIF.

q: What does CIF stand for in trade terms?
r: Cost, Insurance and Freight
The seller pays these to the destination port.

q: Which agency in the U.S. enforces customs laws at the border?
r: U.S. Customs and Border Protection
It inspects goods and collects duties.

q: What is dumping in international trade?
r: Selling goods abroad at prices below their cost or home-market price
Anti-dumping duties may be imposed.
w: Selling goods at a fair price

q: What are anti-dumping duties?
r: Extra tariffs placed on goods sold below fair value
They protect domestic industries.

q: What is an export license?
r: Government permission to export certain goods
It is required for sensitive or controlled items.
w: A license to sell items locally
It is not a tax receipt.

q: A U.S. company wants to ship advanced encryption software abroad. What is most likely required?
r: Compliance with export controls and possibly a license
Sensitive technology is regulated.

q: What does the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) prohibit?
r: Bribing foreign officials to obtain business
It applies to U.S. companies and individuals.

q: A U.S. manager pays an official abroad to speed up a business permit as a favor. Which law is most likely violated?
r: The Foreign Corrupt Practices Act
It bars paying officials for business advantage.

q: What is currency exchange rate?
r: The price of one country's currency in terms of another
It changes with market conditions.

q: If the U.S. dollar becomes stronger against the euro, what happens to U.S. exports to Europe?
r: They become more expensive for European buyers
A stronger dollar makes U.S. goods costlier abroad.
w: They become cheaper for European buyers
This is the effect of a weaker dollar.
Exchange rates do not make exports illegal.

q: A weaker dollar generally makes U.S. exports:
r: More competitive abroad
Foreign buyers pay less in their own currency.
w: This is the effect of a stronger dollar.

q: What is comparative advantage?
r: A country's ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than others
It is the basis for gains from trade.
w: A country's ability to produce everything

q: What is absolute advantage?
r: The ability to produce more of a good with the same resources than another producer
It compares productivity.
w: The ability to produce at a lower opportunity cost

q: What is a joint venture in international business?
r: A partnership in which two or more firms share ownership of a project
It spreads risk and resources.
w: That is not a joint venture.

q: What is foreign direct investment (FDI)?
r: A company investing in operations or assets in another country
Building a factory abroad is an example.
w: A person buying a souvenir abroad
That is a purchase, not investment.
That is lending, not direct investment.
A tariff paid at the border

q: What is a multinational corporation?
r: A company that operates in several countries
It has facilities or subsidiaries abroad.
w: A company that only sells at home

q: What is outsourcing?
r: Contracting work to an outside company, sometimes in another country
It can reduce costs.
w: Opening a new branch in the same city

q: What is a cultural consideration when doing business abroad?
r: Learning local customs, etiquette and communication styles
It helps avoid misunderstandings.

q: What is intellectual property protection abroad?
r: Registering patents and trademarks in each country where protection is needed
Rights are often country by country.
w: Without registration, protection may be weak.
Selling the IP to a competitor

q: What does the WIPO treaty system help with?
r: Protecting intellectual property across countries
It provides common procedures.
w: It does not set currency values.

q: What is the CISG?
r: A United Nations convention governing international sales of goods
It applies when parties are in member countries.
w: It is not a tax form.

q: Two businesses in different countries disagree over a contract. Which clause helps decide which country's law applies?
r: A choice-of-law clause
It names the governing law.
w: It saves valid parts of a contract.

q: What does a force majeure clause do?
r: Excuses performance when extraordinary events outside a party's control occur
Examples include natural disasters and wars.
w: Forces a party to perform no matter what

q: What is an international arbitration clause?
r: A contract term sending disputes to arbitration instead of national courts
It can make enforcement easier across borders.

q: What treaty helps enforce foreign arbitration awards in many countries?
r: The New York Convention
Over 160 countries have joined.

q: What is a trade sanction?
r: A penalty imposed on a country by restricting trade or finance
Sanctions are often used against violations.

q: Which U.S. office administers many economic sanctions?
r: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC)
It is part of the Treasury Department.

q: What is a free trade zone?
r: An area where goods can be imported, stored or processed with reduced duties
It supports international trade.
w: An area where trade is forbidden
An area where goods are given away

q: What does 'Made in USA' labeling law require?
r: The claim must be truthful, meaning products are all or virtually all made in the U.S.
The FTC enforces it.
w: Any product can use the label
Only foreign goods can use it
The label is always optional and false claims are fine
